query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous mechanical and corrosive attack, the tribo-corrosion degradation of high‐entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic formation and disruption of a dense, in situ–formed oxide film (e.g., a spinel-type film enriched in elements like Al and Fe) that acts as a diffusion barrier. When this film is intact, it mitigates both wear by providing a lubricious, hard barrier and corrosion by slowing ion penetration; however, under conditions of repeated mechanical stress the film is periodically removed, exposing fresh metal that undergoes accelerated corrosion and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a composition similar to AlCoCrFeNi or MgAlTiVFeCo, initially presenting a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure with no pre-existing thick or stable oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Pre-form a protective oxide film on one set of samples by high-temperature annealing in an oxygenated environment, while leaving a matched set untreated. Then subject both sets to identical reciprocating sliding tests in a corrosive NaCl solution.
generation.conditions: Identical tribological loading (e.g., constant normal load and sliding speed) and corrosive environment (3.5 wt% NaCl) at ambient or moderately elevated temperatures where oxide formation is kinetically favorable.
generation.structural_mediator: An in situ–formed, continuous oxide film (spinel-type or similar) that forms on the alloy surface and whose integrity governs the exposure of the underlying metal to wear and corrosion.
generation.mechanism: The oxide film acts as a dual-function barrier: it mechanically protects against abrasive wear and, due to its low ion diffusivity, mitigates corrosive attack. However, during sliding, local mechanical disruption of the film exposes fresh alloy areas, which rapidly corrode. The balance between film regeneration and mechanical removal determines the overall tribo-corrosion degradation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples pre-treated to develop an intact oxide film will exhibit lower overall degradation, with reduced wear depth and lower corrosion current density, compared to untreated samples. If the mechanical disruption rate exceeds oxide reformation, both wear and corrosion rates would increase. This coupled effect should be observable as a lower degradation rate in the pre-oxidized group versus the control group.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples without a pre-formed oxide layer, which are expected to show higher combined wear and corrosion degradation due to frequent exposure of fresh, unprotected metal.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments with sufficient oxygen (or oxidizing conditions) where oxide film formation is possible and at loading conditions where the film can partially persist. It may fail in inert atmospheres, extremely high mechanical loads that continuously remove any oxide, or temperatures where oxide kinetics are too slow to form a protective layer.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide film reformation and the relative contributions of mechanical removal versus corrosion propagation under dynamic conditions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples. Pre-treat one group by annealing in an oxygen-rich environment to promote the formation of a dense oxide film while keeping the other group in an inert environment to minimize oxide formation. Subject both groups to identical reciprocating sliding wear tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. Track wear depth, corrosion rates, and the surface integrity of the oxide layer (using microscopy and XPS) over time.
measurements: Surface oxide continuity and composition (via SEM/XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples with the intended intact oxide film do not exhibit significantly lower wear and corrosion degradation compared to the untreated samples, or if no measurable difference in oxide film stability is detected despite the different pre-treatments, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: MgAlTiVFeCo lightweight high-entropy alloy (designated LW850, LW900, LW950, LW1000 based on sintering temperature). System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs.
